title: 144 times a day
hookLine: 144 times a day; putting it face down is a practice

cards: A hundred and forty-four. That's how many times a day, according to one survey of Americans, people check their phones. Spread over sixteen waking hours, it's about once every six or seven minutes.
And there's a decent chance you're listening to this on one. A lot of those checks don't feel like decisions. The hand just goes.

Nobody here is going to tell you to throw it in a lake. It's how you talk to people you love, and it's how you got here today. But today's idea is small and a little radical: putting it face down is a practice.

teach.b: Remember Pascal from yesterday, who traced the unhappiness of men to one fact: "they cannot stay quietly in their own chamber"? He was writing about hunting and gambling and the royal court. He never saw a phone.
But he'd recognize the reach of the hand. In 2017, researchers at the University of Texas ran a simple experiment.
People did tests of attention and memory with their phones either on the desk face down, in a pocket or bag, or in another room. All the phones were silent.
The people whose phones were in another room did best. The phone didn't have to buzz. Just being nearby seemed to pull at part of the mind.

So face down is a start, and the next room is even better. And an old practice already knows this shape. In Jewish tradition, the Sabbath is a day each week when work stops, from sundown Friday to nightfall Saturday.
The rabbi Abraham Joshua Heschel described it as a kind of palace built in time rather than in space: not a place you go, but a stretch of hours you protect.
For Sabbath-observant Jews, the phone is set down with the rest of the week's work. Some people outside Judaism now keep what they call a tech sabbath. You don't have to start with a whole day.
The point isn't that the phone is bad.
The point is that the hand should be yours.

how: Sabbath-observant Jews set phones aside from Friday sundown to Saturday nightfall, and some people of other backgrounds keep a weekly tech sabbath or phone-free meals.

practice: Here's the practice. If you're not listening on your phone, put it face down now, or in a bag. If you are, set it down, screen down, as the bell starts.
Then sit for about forty-five seconds. Notice any pull toward it: the hand, the itch, the thought that something might be waiting. Just notice the pull, and let it pass, like weather.
It'll still be there after the bell.

wordCard.voice: The phone. A tool you love, and a hand that reaches on its own, until you put it face down on purpose. Eleventh word.

orig.note: Hebrew, from Jewish tradition: Sabbath, from a root meaning to stop or rest. A day when work, and for many the phone, is set down.

carryVoice: Your line: face down for three minutes. Three minutes is enough to find out whose hand it is. That's day eleven.
